blocks.text: For years, it had been just Morgan and me.
I was a single mother, and my eleven-year-old son was the center of my world.
We didn’t have a perfect life. Our apartment was small, our furniture was secondhand, and sometimes I had to calculate every dollar before buying groceries.
And somehow, that always felt like enough.

Morgan was the kind of child who could turn an ordinary Tuesday into an adventure. He told terrible jokes, laughed at his own punchlines, and insisted that every dinner deserved dessert, even if dessert was simply a banana.
Every evening, we shared the happiest and most difficult moments of our day.
Morgan always tried to sneak in an extra happy moment.
“Then change the rules, Mom. You’re in charge!”
I loved that boy more than words could explain.
For two weeks, he’d been talking about nothing except the upcoming school fair.
“Mom, they’re going to have pizza, games, prizes, and the biggest cookies you’ve ever seen!”
“Sounds like a very educational experience,” I teased.
I laughed and handed him fifty dollars on the morning of the fair.
“Here. Spend it wisely. And please don’t come home with fifty dollars’ worth of cookies.”
I watched him run toward the school bus, his backpack bouncing against his shoulders.
I had no idea that I was watching him carry the money that would change several lives.
At around two-thirty that afternoon, my phone rang.
“Yes. Is everything okay? Did something happen to Morgan?”
“Your son is safe,” she quickly assured me. “But I need you to come to school immediately.”
Then she whispered, “Please just come. And when you get here, you’ll understand.”
I grabbed my keys and drove straight to the school.
The entire journey, my mind raced through possibilities.
Had he gotten into trouble? Had he broken something? Had he given his money away?
He was supposed to be spending his money on pizza and cookies.
When I arrived, I hurried into the gymnasium.
The school fair had practically come to a standstill.
Children stood in small groups. Several teachers were wiping their eyes. A few parents were gathered around a folding table near the stage.
And there, standing in the middle of everything, was my son.
Before I could answer, Mrs. Bennett approached.
There was a small cardboard box with a handwritten sign.
“FOR ELLIE’S FAMILY. PLEASE HELP THEM COME HOME.”
Beside it lay several receipts, a notebook, and Morgan’s remaining pocket change.
She was quiet, polite, and usually sat near the window.
I’d seen her once or twice during school events, but I didn’t know much about her.
Three weeks earlier, Ellie had stopped coming to school regularly.
At first, everyone assumed she was sick.
Then Mrs. Bennett told the class that Ellie’s father had been seriously injured in a workplace accident.
Her mother had been struggling to pay the bills while caring for him and looking after Ellie’s younger brother.
Eventually, the family had been forced to leave their apartment.
They were staying in temporary accommodation while trying to find somewhere affordable.
Ellie had returned to school, but she was different.
She no longer talked about weekend activities.
And when the other children discussed the school fair, she quietly said she wouldn’t be attending.
“Why aren’t you coming?” he had asked her.
“My mom says we have more important things to worry about.”
And on the morning of the fair, he’d made a decision.
When the fair began, Morgan didn’t rush toward the cookie stand.
He didn’t buy the toy cars he’d been talking about for days.
“Because she needs it more than I need cookies.”
Mrs. Bennett tried to explain that he didn’t have to do that.
Then he asked whether the school could organize a collection for Ellie’s family.
She spoke with the principal, who approved a small voluntary donation table.
He spent the next hour asking classmates whether they wanted to contribute.
Others donated the money they’d planned to spend on games.
A girl donated the five dollars her grandmother had given her.
He went around the gymnasium collecting unopened school supplies, children’s books, and spare winter clothes that families had brought for the school’s donation drive.
By the time I arrived, the cardboard box was nearly full.
“You gave away your entire fifty dollars?”
